This project is an exploration of linear models. Models are estimated by linear regression.  The data set is from Motor Trend magazine.

The assignment is based on estimation of 3 models:
1. mpg as a function of cyl
2. mpg as a function of disp
3  mpg as a function of both cyl and disp

Complete a linear model with data description, a model fit a, and a prediction of mpg based on weigth of 3.050 lbs, with a displacement of 122 cubic inches (this is 2.5 L).

use an anova to compare model 2 with model 3

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
# Load the dataset (built-in)

```{r}
data(mtcars)
require(tigerstats)
require(favstats)
```

# View first 6 rows and summary
```{r}
head(mtcars)
```

# Model 1:
 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) is the predictor (X)

## data summary
### graphical summary

```{r}
plot(mpg~wt,data=mtcars, pch=19)
grid()
```

As the cars weight increases, its fuel efficiency decreases revealing a strong negative correlation. 

### numerical summary


```{r}
cor(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg) 
```

### model summary

```{r}
model1 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
summary(model1)
```


### predicted mpg

```{r}
newData = data.frame(wt=3.050, disp=122)
print(predict(model1, newData, interval = 'predict'))
```
# Model 2:

 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) is the predictor (X)

## data summary
### graphical summary

```{r}
plot(mpg~disp,data=mtcars, pch=19)
grid()
```

As engine displacement increases, fuel efficiency decreases.

### numerical summary

```{r}
cor(mtcars$disp, mtcars$mpg) 
```
### model summary


```{r}
model2 <- lm(mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model2)
```
### predicted mpg 

```{r}
print(predict(model2, newData, interval = 'predict'))
```

# Model 3 :

 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt and disp are the predictors (X's)

## data summary
### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
```

The lighter cars get much better mileage while heavy cars struggle to get past 15. In the displacement and fuel efficiency is shows as the engine volume grows, fuel drops flat. 

### numerical summary

No numerical summary for model 3; two regressors 

### model summary
model3= lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
model summary (coefficients, R², etc.), summarize the fit

```{r}
model3= lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model3)
```
 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) and displacement (disp) are the predictors (X's)

## data summary

### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg ~ wt+disp, data=mtcars)
```

The lighter cars get much better mileage while heavy cars struggle to get past 15. In the displacement and fuel efficiency is shows as the engine volume grows, fuel drops flat.

### numerical summary

No numerical summary for model 3; two regressors

### model summary

```{r}
model3= lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model3)
```

# anova: compare models 2 and 3

model3 <- lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)

model summary (coefficients, R², etc.)
```{r}
summary(model3)
```

### predicted mpg
```{r}
print(predict(model1, newData, interval = 'predict'))
```


```{r}
anova_result <- anova(model1, model3)
print(anova_result)
```

# Discussion and Conculsions

Neither vehicle weight nor engine displacement has any linear relationship with mpg. It doesn't make a difference.
